Reviewer guide · Math Level 3

Thank you for helping again. Math Level 3 of LearnGED is now complete: 24 lessons and 24 practice pages, in English and in Spanish. Level 3 opens the route Prepare for the GED: the rules of exponents, scientific notation, radicals and the real numbers, linear equations and inequalities, formulas, angles, the Pythagorean theorem, similar figures, volume, box plots and histograms, and counting and probability.

A level is marked 🟢 ready only after a GED teacher who teaches in English has reviewed it. The Level 1 guide explains the general style and the Level 2 guide the conventions of the earlier levels; this guide focuses on what is new in Level 3.

1. What to review

Each lesson is the main page (about 4 hours of student work). Its practice page has 3 to 6 activities that make new exercises every time; the lesson links to each one. The Spanish column is there only if you want to compare: both versions are built from the same source, so they must teach exactly the same thing.

2. How to split the work

Nobody needs to read all 48 pages. Two ways that work well:

  • By topic: each reviewer takes one or two topics (3 lessons each) and signs off on them in section 9.
  • By sample: if you have only an hour, read one lesson and its practice page all the way through, and skim the rest of that topic. Good samples: 1.2 (zero and negative exponents), 2.2 (scientific notation with the calculator), 3.1 (simplifying radicals), 4.2 (variables on both sides), 5.1 (inequalities), 6.2 (Pythagorean theorem), 7.2 (box plots), and 8.1 (permutations and combinations).

In each lesson, please try the 8-question quiz at the end, and in each practice page do at least two exercises per activity, including one with a wrong answer on purpose, to see the hint.

↑ Back to top

3. What is new in Level 3

  • Algebra you can see. Exponents are shown as repeated factors that cancel, and equations are solved on a balance scale that shows how each move keeps both sides equal.
  • Answers in more than one form. The practice pages accept equivalent forms where it makes sense (a fraction or a decimal, 36π or a decimal). Scientific notation is typed in two boxes: the number and the power of 10.
  • The calculator in context. The TI-30XS simulator is used with the ×10ⁿ key (scientific notation), the square root, π, and nPr / nCr. Topic 8 insists on telling P from C: does the order matter?
  • Figures drawn by the page. Angles with a transversal, right triangles, similar figures, solids, box plots, and histograms are drawn with their measurements, and each has a text description for screen readers.
  • Explore pages for geometry and probability (see the list above), and a review of the whole level in the practice page of Lesson 8.3.
  • Final project and final check. The project is a small investigation with the student's own data; the final check has 25 questions.
↑ Back to top

4. What to look for

  • Reading level. The algebra is harder here, but the sentences should not be. Mark any word or sentence that is too hard.
  • Tone. Our students are adults. Does anything sound childish, or too academic?
  • Math accuracy. Numbers, signs, rounding, units, and every step of the worked examples.
  • US usage. Anything that sounds translated or “not how we say it here” (see the questions in section 8).
  • Hints. Do the hints name the likely mistake without giving the answer away?
  • Answer checking. If you type a correct answer in another reasonable form and the page rejects it, please tell us what you typed.
  • Figures and graphs. Labels that overlap a line or a number on an axis, points in the wrong place, colors that are hard to tell apart.
  • Accessibility. Try the pages on a phone and with the keyboard only (the interactive graphs work with the arrow keys too).
↑ Back to top

5. How feedback works

The same idea as in Levels 1 and 2: a mistake is information, not a failure.

  1. First wrong answer: a hint that points to the specific mistake (for example, “When you multiply both sides by a negative number, the inequality sign flips.”). The student tries again.
  2. Second wrong answer: the solution, explained step by step.
  3. Questions with only two choices (for example, “does the order matter: permutation or combination?”) show the explanation right away, because a second try would be a guess.
  4. Praise is about the strategy, not about being smart.

6. Math conventions

TopicLearnGED
ExponentsFinal answers use positive exponents: x⁻³ is written 1/x³.
Scientific notationa × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10, typed in two boxes (3.2 and 5 for 3.2 × 10⁵). On the TI-30XS, the key is ×10ⁿ.
RadicalsSimplest form: 3√2, not √18 (no perfect-square factor left under the root). The decimal from the calculator is used to check the answer.
Real numbersNatural, whole, integer, rational, and irrational, shown as nested sets and on the number line.
EquationsVariables on both sides; special cases are named “no solution” and “all real numbers (infinitely many solutions)”.
Inequalities<, >, ≤, ≥. On the number line: open circle for < and >, closed circle for ≤ and ≥. The sign flips when both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number.
Formulas“Solve the formula for…” (for example, solve d = rt for t). The letters are those of the GED formula sheet.
AnglesDegrees. Pairs: complementary, supplementary, vertical, corresponding, alternate interior, alternate exterior.
Pythagorean theorema² + b² = c², c is the hypotenuse; the converse tells whether a triangle is a right triangle.
Similar figuresScale factor and proportions; scale drawings use inches, feet, and miles.
VolumeV = Bh for prisms and cylinders; π answers as 36π or as a decimal. US units: cubic inches, cubic feet, gallons.
QuartilesMethod of halves: Q1 is the median of the lower half and Q3 the median of the upper half; with an odd number of data, the median goes into neither half. IQR = Q3 − Q1.
HistogramsEqual intervals (bins); the left end is included and the right end is not, unless the page says otherwise.
CountingCounting principle, nPr = n!/(n − r)!, nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Probability accepted as a fraction, a decimal, or a percent.

8. Questions for you

  1. Positive exponents. We ask for final answers with positive exponents only (1/x³, not x⁻³). Is that how you grade?
  2. Radicals. We ask for simplest form (3√2) and use the calculator decimal as a check. Do your students need simplest form for the GED, or is a decimal from the calculator enough?
  3. Scientific notation. Is “×10ⁿ key” the name your students use for that key on the TI-30XS?
  4. Quartiles. We use the method of halves (the median goes into neither half). Is that the method you teach?
  5. “Thales' theorem” (title of Lesson 6.3) is common in Latin America. Would you rather call it only “similar triangles and scale drawings”?
  6. “Literal equations” or “solving formulas”? Which one do your students hear more (Lesson 5.3)?
  7. Permutations and combinations. Many students confuse nPr and nCr. Is the question “does the order matter?” enough, or do you use another rule of thumb?
  8. Final check. 25 questions, passing score 18 (72%). Is that a fair bar before Level 4?

10. How to send comments

Any format is fine: an email, a list, or a screenshot with notes. Please say which page, which section (sections and activities are numbered), and, for exercises, what you typed: the practice exercises change every time, so a screenshot helps a lot. Send your comments to José M. Fernández (Zhema).

If you also teach science, social studies, or reading and writing, the page What comes next shows the plan for those subjects, and your ideas are welcome there too.
